title: Episode 125: Martin Van Buren and the Panic of 1837: The Crucible of Martin Van Ruin
description:
When Martin Van Buren was inaugurated as the eighth President of the United States in March eighteen thirty-seven, he seemed to inherit an era of boundless national prosperity. The national debt had been completely paid off under Andrew Jackson, western land sales were booming, and hundreds of state banks were flooding the economy with paper money. Yet beneath this gilded veneer lay a ticking economic bomb.

Just five weeks into Van Buren's term, the bubble burst with catastrophic fury. On May tenth, eighteen thirty-seven, every bank in New York City ran out of gold and silver coin, slammed their doors, and suspended specie payments. A devastating financial contagion swept the nation. Over eight hundred banks collapsed, thousands of businesses went bankrupt, factories shuttered, and bread riots erupted on the streets of Manhattan. Whig critics viciously scapegoated the President, rechristening him 'Martin Van Ruin.'

While political rivals urged Van Buren to revive a private national bank or bail out speculative financiers with paper currency, Van Buren stood immovable. Guided by Jeffersonian principles, he argued that the federal government had no constitutional authority to bail out private speculation. Instead, Van Buren waged a lonely, heroic four-year crusade to create the Independent Treasury System—divorcing the federal government completely from private banking cartels and safeguarding public revenues in federal vaults. Join George as he brings to life the darkest financial trial of the early republic and the birth of modern American fiscal independence.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our journey through the presidency of Martin Van Buren with the supreme crisis that defined his administration: the Panic of eighteen thirty-seven. Just weeks after taking office, Van Buren was hit by the worst financial crash the young nation had ever seen. Banks collapsed, unemployment soared, and angry mobs marched in the streets. Through four years of brutal political attacks, Van Buren refused easy bailouts, fighting tooth and nail to establish a financial system that would protect the public treasury forever. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GILDED MIRAGE
On March fourth, eighteen thirty-seven, Martin Van Buren stood on the east portico of the United States Capitol to take the oath of office as President. The day was sunny, crisp, and filled with triumphant celebration. At Van Buren's side rode the departing hero, Andrew Jackson, whose popularity remained colossal. In his inaugural address, Van Buren marveled at the unprecedented prosperity of the young republic. For the first and only time in American history, the national debt had been paid off down to the last penny, leaving a massive financial surplus in the federal treasury.
Yet beneath the surface of this golden age, the American economy was intoxicated on wild, unregulated speculation. When Andrew Jackson destroyed the Second Bank of the United States in the famous Bank War, federal deposits were distributed among dozens of politically favored state-chartered private banks, derisively dubbed 'pet banks.' Freed from central bank restraint, these state banks printed vast oceans of unbacked paper bank notes, lending money recklessly to land speculators.
Millions of acres of public lands in Michigan, Illinois, and Mississippi were purchased not by actual settlers, but by speculators using worthless paper promises. Canal companies, turnpike corporations, and state governments borrowed tens of millions of dollars from British investors, building unneeded infrastructure in virgin wilderness. Cotton prices soared to record highs on speculative euphoria. The entire nation was living in a glittering, precarious house of paper cards, waiting for a single gust of wind to blow it down.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE DELUGE: MAY 1837
The gust of wind arrived from across the Atlantic. In late eighteen thirty-six, the Bank of England, facing its own catastrophic drain of gold reserves, raised interest rates and sharply curtailed credit to American merchant houses. British investors demanded immediate repayment of loans in solid gold bullion. Simultaneously, Andrew Jackson had struck a mortal blow to the paper system with his famous executive order, the Specie Circular, mandating that the federal government would accept only gold and silver coin—never paper bank notes—for purchases of public lands on the western frontier.
The combination was fatal. In April eighteen thirty-seven, prominent cotton brokerage houses in New Orleans collapsed, dragging down planters and merchant banks across the South. The panic rushed north along rail and telegraph corridors like an express train. Depositors panicked, forming frantic, weeping mobs outside banks in Philadelphia, Baltimore, Boston, and New York, waving fists full of colorful paper notes and desperately demanding redemption in hard gold eagles and Spanish silver dollars.
On the morning of May tenth, eighteen thirty-seven, the financial heart of America stopped beating. Every bank in New York City, having completely exhausted its gold vaults, slammed its heavy iron doors and suspended specie payments. Within days, more than eight hundred banks across the United States suspended payments or closed permanently. Paper currency became overnight garbage; merchant ships rotted at their docks; construction halted on hundreds of canals and railroads; and cotton plummeted from twenty cents a pound to eight cents. Nine out of ten factories in the East closed, throwing thousands into the streets without wages. America had plunged headlong into its first great, systemic economic depression.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: BREAD, BLOOD, AND MARTIN VAN RUIN
The human cost of the Panic of eighteen thirty-seven was catastrophic. In the major cities of the Eastern seaboard, nearly one-third of the urban workforce was thrown into immediate, destitute unemployment. In New York City alone, over fifty thousand workers had no income, no savings, and no food. The price of flour and pork skyrocketed as greedy hoarders locked grain in warehouses, waiting for prices to rise further.
In Manhattan, thousands of starving citizens gathered in City Hall Park under black banners reading 'Bread, Meat, Rent, and Fuel!' Mob leaders pointed toward the great merchant warehouse of Eli Hart and Company on Washington Street, where fifty-three thousand barrels of flour were being hoarded for ransom. The crowd stormed the building, smashing doors with crowbars, tossing hundreds of barrels of flour and sacks of wheat into the street, and battling armed police and the state militia in what became known as the Great Flour Riots. Similar violent bread riots erupted in Philadelphia, Baltimore, and Boston, while destitute families froze in unheated tenements.
The Whig opposition party, led by Henry Clay and Daniel Webster, seized upon the economic misery with vicious, partisan glee. They blamed the entire catastrophe on the policies of Jackson and Van Buren. Whig newspapers baptized the President with a derisive moniker that stuck like tar: 'Martin Van Ruin.' Whig cartoonists portrayed Van Buren lounging inside the White House in silk dressing gowns, sipping champagne from French crystal and eating with gold spoons, while honest American mechanics and their children starved in gutters. Whigs demanded that the President immediately call Congress into session, recharter a national bank, and distribute federal relief to bankrupt businesses.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: VAN BUREN'S PRINCIPLE: THE LIMITS OF GOVERNMENT
In September eighteen thirty-seven, President Martin Van Buren summoned Congress into a special emergency session. The political pressure upon him was immense. Many leaders in his own Democratic Party pleaded with him to yield, print federal paper money, or restore alliances with private state banks. But Van Buren held fast to a strict, philosophical understanding of the Constitution.
In a courageous, masterly message to Congress, Van Buren laid out his diagnosis of the crisis. He refused to apologize for Jackson's hard-money policies. The panic, Van Buren argued, was not caused by federal regulations, but by the reckless greed, over-banking, and gambling spirit of private speculators who had built paper empires on debt. Most controversially, Van Buren asserted that the federal government was not an insurance agency for private misfortune.
In words that became a foundational text of nineteenth-century classical liberalism, Van Buren wrote: 'All communities are apt to look to government for too much. But it is not the legitimate object of government to aid individuals in the pursuit of private speculation, or to repair losses incurred through improvidence. The less government interferes with private pursuits, the better for the general prosperity. Its real duty is to preserve peace, protect property, and leave every citizen free to exert his own industry.' Van Buren refused to bail out the banking cartels. Instead, he proposed a radical, permanent cure: the complete divorce of Bank and State.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE DIVORCE OF BANK AND STATE
Van Buren's revolutionary proposal was the 'Independent Treasury'—often referred to by contemporaries as the 'Sub-Treasury System.' For forty years, the federal government had deposited its tax revenues and customs receipts directly into private banks, which used those public funds as collateral to inflate their own speculative loans. When the banks collapsed in May eighteen thirty-seven, millions of dollars of federal money were trapped and frozen inside their locked vaults.
Van Buren declared that the American people's money should never again be used to fuel private speculation. He proposed that the federal government build its own secure vaults in Washington, New York, Boston, Charleston, and New Orleans. Federal customs collectors and postmasters would deposit public revenues directly into these federal vaults in gold and silver coin. The government would pay its debts solely in hard specie, operating entirely independently of private banks.
The banking establishment and the Whig Party reacted with apocalyptic rage. Henry Clay took to the Senate floor, shouting that the Independent Treasury was a tyrannical scheme to hoard the nation's gold, starve private business of credit, and reduce the American people to poverty. Conservative Democrats, closely tied to state banks, bolted the party to oppose the bill. For three agonizing years, the Independent Treasury bill was passed by the Senate, defeated by the House, reintroduced, and filibustered in one of the longest, most bitter legislative wars in American history.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE TRIUMPH OF THE SUB-TREASURY
Throughout the grueling three-year struggle, Martin Van Buren never flinched. Demonstrating the tactical patience and quiet resilience that had earned him the title of 'The Little Magician,' he systematically rebuilt his coalition. He won over his former bitter rival, John C. Calhoun of South Carolina, by convincing him that an independent federal treasury was the ultimate bulwark of states' rights against Northern financial monopolies.
Finally, in June eighteen forty, after three failed attempts, the Independent Treasury Act passed the House of Representatives by a vote of one hundred and seven to one hundred and seven, with the Speaker casting the deciding vote. On July fourth, eighteen forty—the sixty-fourth anniversary of the Declaration of Independence—President Martin Van Buren signed the bill into law with solemn pride. Democrats celebrated the date as America's second Declaration of Independence: the declaration of financial independence from private banking empires.
The Independent Treasury was an institutional milestone. It established the principle that public funds belong to the public alone, protected from private greed. Though the Whigs temporarily repealed the law in eighteen forty-one, President James K. Polk reenacted it permanently in eighteen forty-six. The Independent Treasury served as the bedrock operating foundation of American federal finance for over seventy years, until it was evolved into the modern Federal Reserve System in nineteen thirteen.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE STATESMAN WHO CHOSE PRINCIPLE OVER RE-ELECTION
While the Independent Treasury was a triumph of principled governance, it came at the ultimate political cost for Martin Van Buren. The American public was exhausted by years of economic depression, high unemployment, and tight credit. Voters did not want lectures on fiscal discipline or constitutional limits; they wanted relief, optimism, and someone to blame.
In the presidential election of eighteen forty, the Whig Party unleashed an unprecedented political carnival against the President, nominating military hero William Henry Harrison. Van Buren was buried under an avalanche of hard cider barrels, miniature log cabins, and catchy campaign jingles mocking 'Van, Van, is a used-up man.' Harrison defeated Van Buren in a landslide, winning two hundred and thirty-four electoral votes to Van Buren's sixty.
Van Buren accepted his defeat with aristocratic grace and philosophical peace. He refused to compromise his convictions to win an election. Later in life, Van Buren made another courageous moral stand, breaking with the Democratic Party in eighteen forty-eight to run for President on the Free Soil ticket, opposing the expansion of slavery into Western territories.
Martin Van Buren proved that true political leadership is not measured merely by holding onto power. In the crucible of America's first great depression, the Red Fox of Kinderhook chose principle over popularity, safeguarded the republic's treasury, and proved that a democratic statesman must sometimes endure the wrath of his contemporaries to protect the liberties of future generations.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Martin Van Buren's steadfast handling of the Panic of eighteen thirty-seven cemented the financial independence of the United States government. Though it cost him his presidency, his creation of the Independent Treasury stood the test of time. Next week, we turn to the man who defeated him: America's ninth President, William Henry Harrison, and the legendary Log Cabin campaign of eighteen forty—a rollicking political carnival that ended with the shortest and most tragic presidency in American history. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
